title: Subqueries: The Basics
description: Nest a SELECT inside another query using subqueries in WHERE, IN, ANY/ALL, and FROM clauses. Learn how SQL Server evaluates nested queries.

data.text: A subquery is a SELECT statement nested inside another statement — inside WHERE, inside another SELECT, or even inside a FROM clause. Subqueries let you break a complex problem into smaller, more readable pieces.
The *inner query* (subquery) runs first and produces a result. The *outer query* uses that result. Every subquery must be wrapped in parentheses, and SQL Server supports up to 32 levels of nesting.

data.caption: A subquery runs first and produces a result set that the outer query depends on
data.definition:
flowchart LR
  Outer[Outer Query
SELECT FROM orders
WHERE customer_id IN (subquery)] --> Sub[(Subquery
SELECT customer_id
FROM customers
WHERE city = 'New York')]
  Sub --> Result[Result: list of customer IDs]
  Result --> Outer

  style Outer fill:#ddf4ff
  style Sub fill:#d1f3d8
  style Result fill:#fff8c5

data.title: Find orders from New York customers
data.code:
SELECT order_id, order_date, customer_id
FROM   sales.orders
WHERE  customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM   sales.customers
    WHERE  city = 'New York'
)
ORDER BY order_date DESC;

data.title: IN vs. EXISTS
data.text: When the subquery references the outer query's table (a correlated subquery), EXISTS is usually more efficient than IN — and safer with NULLs. For a non-correlated subquery that returns a small result, IN and a JOIN are roughly equivalent.
A *scalar subquery* returns exactly one value (one row, one column). You can use it anywhere an expression is allowed — including as a column in a SELECT list.

data.title: Scalar subquery as a column
data.code:
SELECT order_id,
       order_date,
       (
           SELECT MAX(list_price)
           FROM   sales.order_items i
           WHERE  i.order_id = o.order_id
       ) AS max_item_price
FROM   sales.orders o
ORDER BY order_date DESC;

data.text: ANY and ALL compare a scalar expression against a set of values returned by a subquery. ANY returns TRUE if the comparison is true for at least one value; ALL returns TRUE if it is true for every value.

data.title: ANY — greater than any brand's max price
data.code:
SELECT product_name, list_price
FROM   production.products
WHERE  list_price >= ANY (
    SELECT AVG(list_price)
    FROM   production.products
    GROUP BY brand_id
);

data.title: ALL — greater than or equal to every brand's average
data.code:
SELECT product_name, list_price
FROM   production.products
WHERE  list_price >= ALL (
    SELECT AVG(list_price)
    FROM   production.products
    GROUP BY brand_id
);

data.text: You can place a subquery in the FROM clause. The result becomes a derived table (virtual table) that the outer query can select from. It must have an alias.

data.title: Derived table in FROM
Derived tables need aliases
data.text: Any subquery in the FROM clause must be given an alias (e.g., 'AS t'). SQL Server requires it — you will get a syntax error otherwise.

data.title: Subquery essentials
points: A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another query; always wrap it in parentheses
Use IN to match against a list of values from a subquery
Scalar subqueries return one value and can appear in SELECT or WHERE
ANY returns true for at least one match; ALL requires every value to match
Subqueries in FROM become derived tables and require an alias
